newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia blue chips close at 21-month low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia blue chips close at 21-month low.

text.p: Malaysian shares fell sharply on Monday as foreign funds sold off and calls on leveraged investors to pay up hammered the main indices to their lowest levels in 21 months, dealers and fund managers said.
The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index closed down 30.22 points, or 3.24 percent, at a 21-month low of 902.14.
The small-capitalised Second Board index slumped 5.61 percent, or 28.60 points, to 480.86.
"All hell's breaking lose," said a dealing manager at a local brokerage. "It seems like foreigners want to get out of the ringgit."
"Almost everybody agrees that 880 is the next support level. There is only limited support around 900," he said.
At 0729 GMT, the index dipped to 896.59 before local funds came in to support it, dealers said.
A stock index futures dealer at another local brokerage said he had seen "massive selling by foreign funds".
"There has been some nibbling here and there, but they (local funds) are not going in with any gusto," said the futures dealer.
Dealers said large numbers of cash calls on clients accounts also added to the pounding on share prices.
"There is a lot of foreign selling, but the rest is forced selling, including some selling by banks and even the local funds on their clients shares held as collateral," said the dealing manager.
Weakness in the local currency was yet another factor causing the bearishness, said market observers.

The ringgit fell to a 42-month low of 2.73 against the U.S. dollar in late afternoon trading in Kuala Lumpur as sales from offshore investors went virtually unchallenged, foreign exchange dealers said.
"It should be cheaper (for foreigners) to buy (shares) on the one hand, but they would want to see a healthy economy before they come in," said the dealing manager.
Among the hardest-hit issues were key blue-chip stocks such as power utility Tenaga Nasional and Telekom Malaysia, which fell 45 and 30 cents, respectively.
"I have heard that foreigners have been selling. I don't quite know why it has taken them so long," said Hugh Young, managing director of Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore.
Young said the selling was mainly due to exchange rate uncertainty, "elements of a bubble economy", and borrowing for the construction of large infrastructure projects.
"A lot of the drivers of the economy have been margin lending," said Young. "It is a virtuous circle when things are going up, but a vicious one when coming down," he added.

Young said he had reduced Aberdeen's exposure to Malaysia to around eight percent of their funds in Asia, excluding Japan, from a peak of 19 percent. Dealers and fund managers said the outlook remained gloomy.
"The worst is yet to come," said the futures trader.
Companies in the finance sector were among the heaviest traded. RHB Capital, MBf Capital and Public Bank all fell between 16 and 35 cents on heavy volumes.
Analysts said the exposure of banking and finance stocks to exchange rate fluctuations and margin calls made them especially vulnerable.
Overall market volume stood at 259 million shares, valued at 1,284 million ringgit. Losers trounced gainers 722 to 25.

On the Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange, the spot August contract fell 35.5 points to 925.5 with 1,502 lots traded. September futures closed 35.2 points lower, also at 925.5, with 16 lots having changed hands.
